name: APTOS thread lift

lead: APTOS threads are barbed polypropylene sutures inserted under facial skin to support sagging tissue without a surgical facelift. They are typically promoted for the cheeks, jowls and jawline and form part of the broader thread-lift category.

Early reports from the originator's group describe improvement in contour in a series of 186 patients. Later literature includes case reports of complications and small retrospective studies of combined treatments.

paras: Sharp dents or barbs along each thread grip the tissue; the thread is anchored so that it holds the tissue in a higher position. Some authors describe stimulating tissue response around the thread as well.

Reported problems include thread migration and partial expulsion; a MACS facelift has been used to correct APTOS complications. Wikipedia notes that UK practitioners face no mandatory qualification and cites a physician quoted by the BBC describing thread lifts as potentially causing irreversible damage.

lead: APTOS threads are barbed non-absorbable sutures, originally made of polypropylene with dents along their length, used to lift ptotic facial tissue without a facelift.[1] The technique was described in 2002 by a group who used them in 186 patients and reported success in lifting various areas and improving facial contour.[1]

A 2004 review describes self-retaining barbed sutures as innovations for nonsurgical facial and neck rejuvenation available as short APTOS threads or long WOFFLES threads; its author uses APTOS for malar rounding and firming and WOFFLES as a sling to temporal scalp tissue.[2] A 2005 chapter describes the approach as the featherlift.[3]

Complications are documented in case literature, including thread migration and partial expulsion.[4] Wikipedia notes that UK aesthetic practitioners need no mandatory qualification and reports a BBC investigation of short low-cost training courses.[5] Evidence is mainly case series and retrospective studies, plus small registered trials without published results found.

paras: The original APTOS sutures were polypropylene threads modified with many dents along their length so the sharp edges hold tissue firmly.[1] Short threads are used for areas such as the cheeks, while longer threads act as slings anchored to firm tissue.[2] More recent products include absorbable poly-L-lactic acid and polycaprolactone threads.[6]

Reports describe using APTOS threads for malar rounding, facial tightening, jawline and marionette line correction (with a collagen-stimulating filler),[2][7] and, in a 2025 retrospective study, non-surgical otoplasty.[8] A 2026 paper describes a suture-crossing technique for contour restoration.[6]

A 2005 case report described migration and partial expulsion of an Aptos thread after initially successful fixation.[4] A 2012 report used a MACS lift and fat grafting to treat a complication from APTOS sutures. Wikipedia describes a BBC report quoting a physician who called thread lifts among the most dangerous aesthetic procedures, with possible irreversible damage.[5]

The 2002 series of 186 patients is the founding report and was authored by the technique's developers.[1] Registered trials include a completed study of HA-coated versus non-HA threads for midface lifting and nasolabial fold correction (n=144)[9] and a study combining thread lifting and microfocused ultrasound (n=45, status unknown).[10] No published results from these were found. No randomized trials establishing longevity were found.
